# Walking Meetings: 7 Ways to Add Movement to Your Workday (Even on Zoom)


Last updated November 2026


Inbox on the laptop, Alpine trail on the screen. The WalkDesk turns the Podium into a walking desk.


**Short answer:** A walking meeting is a meeting you hold while walking instead of sitting around a table. The science backs them: Stanford researchers found walking boosted creative thinking for 81% of the people they tested, and a Columbia trial found that 5 minutes of light walking every 30 minutes blunted blood-sugar rises over a long sitting day. The easiest ways to start are to walk your one-on-ones, take listen-only calls on your feet, stand for group meetings and put video calls on a treadmill at a slow 1 to 2 mph.


The catch is that people rarely follow through. When Danish researchers offered office workers walking meetings, almost nobody took them. Weather, laptops, groups of three or more and the nagging feeling of skipping work all got in the way. Each of the seven ideas below gets around at least one of those problems, and the last few still work when every meeting on your calendar is a video call.


## In this article


- Do walking meetings actually work?

## Do Walking Meetings Actually Work? What the Science Says


Yes, for the right kind of meeting. Five studies are worth knowing:


Study What they tested What they found


[Stanford, 2014](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24749966/) Creative-thinking tests while sitting, then walking on a treadmill or outdoors Walking raised creative output for 81% of participants, and the boost lingered after they sat back down


[Columbia, 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36728338/) 8 hours of sitting, broken up by light walks of different lengths, in 11 middle-aged and older adults Only 5 minutes every 30 minutes significantly blunted the blood-sugar rise. Every break schedule lowered blood pressure


[Mayo Clinic, 2007](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17504789/) Computer work at a treadmill desk vs. an office chair, in 15 adults with obesity Walking at a self-chosen 1.1 mph burned about 119 more calories an hour


[Brigham Young, 2015](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25874910/) Memory, attention and typing tests at 1.5 mph vs. sitting Small dips in learning and typing. Recall stayed the same


[Southern Denmark, 2020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32151044/) Standing and walking meetings in real offices Regular standing meetings cut 59 minutes of sitting per 8-hour workday. Walking meetings rarely happened


Walking helps when you're talking, listening or coming up with ideas, and it costs you a little on typing and number-crunching. A[University of Tennessee study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19953838/) measured a 6 to 11% drop in mouse skills and math scores on a treadmill desk, while attention and reading comprehension held steady. A[2020 review of 18 studies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32116273/) on treadmill and cycling desks found typing slowed down while attention held up. So walk the conversations, and sit or stand for the spreadsheets.


## Why Do Most Walking Meetings Never Happen?


In the Danish "Take a Stand!" trial, offices mapped out walking routes and 89% of participants knew where to find them. Walking meetings still barely happened.[The researchers](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7084221/) heard the same practical complaints over and over:


- The weather
- Needing to take notes or look at a computer
- Walking and talking with more than two people
- No privacy on a public sidewalk
- Extra prep time
- Worrying that leaving the building looks like skipping work


Every item on that list is a logistics problem, and logistics problems can be planned around.


## How Do You Add Movement to Your Workday? 7 Ways


### 1. Walk Your One-on-Ones


Two people is the sweet spot. Add a third and somebody ends up trailing behind, shouting into the wind. Pick a loop you already know that takes about as long as the meeting, say 20 or 30 minutes, so nobody has to check the time. Send over the one or two questions you want to settle beforehand, because there's no slide deck to lean on. And save the sensitive stuff (pay, performance, anything personal) for a quiet route or a closed door.


### 2. Brainstorm on Your Feet, Write It Up Sitting Down


The Stanford team found that walking helps idea generation while you're moving and for a while afterward, and the desk studies show typing is what suffers. So split the meeting in two. Walk while you throw ideas around, then sit down for the last five minutes to write up decisions and who owns what. A voice memo on your phone (with everyone's OK) catches the good stuff said mid-stride.


### 3. Walk the Calls You Only Need to Hear


All-hands, webinars, the weekly update where you're on mute for 40 minutes: these were made for walking. Turn the camera off, pop in your earbuds and head outside. If it's pouring or freezing (weather was the first barrier the Danish researchers listed), take the call to a treadmill instead.


### 4. Put Your Video Calls on a Treadmill (Yes, Even on Zoom)


This is the version that survives winter, back-to-back calendars and the need for a laptop. A treadmill desk keeps your notes in front of you while you walk, and since you never leave your desk, nobody wonders where you went. Here's the setup:


- Keep it slow, around 1 to 2 mph. People in the Mayo Clinic study picked 1.1 mph on their own, and the BYU study used 1.5 mph. That's enough to count as moving and slow enough that nobody hears you breathing.
- Keep the belt at 0 to 2% incline while you're talking, and save the hills for later.
- Put the camera on something level. A laptop on a steady desk surface beats a phone in your hand, because nobody wants to watch your call from a boat.
- Wear a headset or earbuds with a mic. Keeping the mic near your mouth favors your voice over your footsteps.
- Save your call speed to a shortcut. The speed keys on Aviron's Justice and Podium are customizable, so one tap takes you straight to meeting pace.


The treadmill itself stays quiet on a call: Aviron's brushless motors run at roughly 40 dB at walking speed, about the background noise of an average home. ### 5. Stand for the Meetings You Can't Walk


Group calls, screen shares and anything involving a whiteboard don't walk well. Stand for those instead. In the Danish trial, people who stood for meetings regularly sat 59 fewer minutes per 8-hour workday, and they rated standing meetings as more focused. With a treadmill desk, just stop the belt and you've got a standing desk.


### 6. Take 5 Every 30


Back-to-back calls are where sitting time piles up. In the Columbia trial, 5 minutes of light walking every 30 minutes was the only schedule that significantly blunted blood-sugar rises. The easiest way to fit that in is to make your calendar end meetings early.[Google Calendar](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/11/schedule-meetings-with-default-buffer-google-calendar.html) (the setting used to be called Speedy meetings) and[Outlook](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/build-in-time-between-back-to-back-meetings-14f7be15-3913-4d40-90c7-6f9e67ded46b) can both shorten new meetings automatically. Then use the gap for a lap around the block or a few minutes on the treadmill. Guard the walk after lunch too: here's[why a short walk after eating helps](https://www.avironactive.com/blog/walking-after-eating/) .


### 7. Save the Real Workout for After Your Last Call


A 1.5 mph desk walk is light activity. It's great for breaking up sitting, but it won't get you fit on its own, and the[US guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/adults.html) still call for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. Luckily, the treadmill under your desk is a full-size one, so when you close the laptop after your last call, it's ready for a brisk walk, a run or a climb.


That's also the point where a lot of home treadmills lose their owners. Week one is fun. By month two, it's an expensive clothes rack. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is a walking meeting?


A meeting held while walking instead of sitting, usually between two people, outdoors or on a treadmill. It works best for one-on-ones, brainstorms and calls where you mostly talk or listen.


### How many steps is a 30-minute walking meeting?


About 3,000 at a brisk pace.[Researchers use 100 steps a minute](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30654810/) as the marker for moderate-intensity walking, so 30 minutes at that cadence comes to about 3,000 steps. At a slow treadmill-desk pace, expect fewer.


### Are treadmill desks good for you?


For breaking up long stretches of sitting, yes. In a small Mayo Clinic study, walking at about 1 mph while working burned roughly 119 more calories an hour than sitting. Expect your typing to slow down a little, and keep doing proper workouts as well.


### Can people hear a treadmill on a video call?


At walking speed, not much. Aviron's brushless motors run at about 40 dB when you're walking, roughly the background noise of a home. A headset mic close to your mouth makes the biggest difference, and so does keeping the belt slow and flat.


### Are standing meetings better than walking meetings?


For groups, often. In the Danish "Take a Stand!" trial, standing meetings caught on and cut sitting time, while walking meetings rarely happened. Walk your one-on-ones and listen-only calls, and stand for groups and screen shares.


### What speed should you walk at a treadmill desk?


Start around 1 to 1.5 mph, then go up 0.1 mph at a time until you can still talk and type comfortably. In the studies above, desk walkers chose or were set at 1.1 to 1.5 mph.
